Who handles the invoices today?
Who do you send them to?
What happens when a supplier changes the format?
What do you do when a supplier changes the format?
Before you show me anything: how much do you already know about how we work?
Almost nothing, and that is exactly why I asked for this call. Who handles the invoices today?
Four people in finance. Two of them do nothing else, and both of them have been here longer than I have.
And what happens when a supplier changes the format?
Somebody notices three days later, and then we fix it by hand. It is a workaround, and it has been the same workaround for six years.
How long does the month-end closing take you?
Nine working days. It should be four. That is the number my board asks me about, and it is the reason I took this call.
Then one more before I say anything about us. What do those nine days cost you, apart from the time?
Who handles that today?
What happens when the process fails?
How long does the closing take today?
How many people work on it every month?
Who asks you about that number?

I do not demo on a first call. I do not even open the file, and I have stopped apologising for it. The moment a deck is on the screen, the customer stops describing their own problem and starts reacting to my product, and I have never once got the original description back. What I am listening for is two things, and only two. A number and a workaround. A number gives the problem a size: nine days instead of four, eleven steps instead of six, four people instead of one. And a workaround tells me the problem has been there long enough for somebody to build a habit around it, which means somebody has been quietly paying for it every month for years. The last thing, and this is the one that took me longest to learn: after you ask a question, say nothing. The silence is where the useful half of the answer lives. Filling it is the most expensive habit in this job.

I take a lot of these calls, and there is one question almost nobody asks me. Nobody asks what happens today when the process fails. They ask what I want to buy, they ask what my priorities are for next year, they ask about budget in the first ten minutes, and then they tell me about their platform. The ones I remember asked me to walk them through the last time it went wrong. When somebody arrives with the solution already prepared, I can hear it in the first three minutes, because they are selling to a company they invented on the way to the meeting, and it is never quite mine. And here is the part that would surprise them. Some of our worst problems have been there for years and have never been escalated, because escalating something means admitting that it has been normal for a long time. So it stays, everybody works around it, and no vendor ever hears about it, because no vendor ever asks.
